primer.title: A website
primer.body: A website is a set of pages stored on a computer called a server. When you open one, your browser asks that server for the page and shows you what comes back.

primer.title: A server
primer.body: A server is a computer that stays switched on and answers requests from other computers. That is why a website still works when your own laptop is off.

primer.title: An API
primer.body: An API is a doorway that lets one program ask another for something, like ‘send this SMS’ or ‘give me this customer’s orders’. You can think of it as a menu: it lists what you may ask for.

primer.title: A database
primer.body: A database is an organised store of information, like a spreadsheet that apps can read and update instantly. Orders, customers and messages live there.

primer.title: An AI model
primer.body: An AI model is software trained on huge amounts of text that predicts a helpful reply to what you type. It can be wrong, so we always check what it says.

lesson.title: The idea trap
lesson.body_md:
A few years ago, having a clever business idea involving software was rare, because building it needed a team. Today you can type a request into an AI tool and get a working first version in an afternoon. That is exciting, but it has a side effect: everyone else can do it too.

Picture a student in Yaba who thinks, “I will build a bot that takes orders on WhatsApp for food vendors.” By the time they open their laptop, other people in Abuja, Accra and Nairobi have typed almost the same sentence. When an idea can be copied in a day, the idea itself stops being the thing that protects you or earns you money.

This does not mean ideas are useless. A good idea tells you where to look. It just isn’t enough on its own. The rest of this module is about what is enough.

**In simple terms:** If everyone can build the same thing quickly, then having the idea first is not an advantage.

**Go deeper:** Economists call this a collapse in the cost of production. When production becomes cheap, value moves to what stays scarce: trust, reliability, distribution and knowing the customer’s problem deeply.
lesson.story_md: In a scenario where two friends both think of the same idea, a WhatsApp ordering bot for food vendors, one of them spends three months planning the perfect version, with a logo, a pitch and a long list of features. The other builds a rough version in one week and gives it to three vendors on their street. By the time the first friend is ready to launch, the second already knows which vendors forget to reply, which customers send voice notes instead of text, and which feature nobody uses.
lesson.story_lesson: The idea was identical. What separated them was how fast each one met a real customer.
lesson.check_prompt: Why does a good idea protect you less than it used to?

check_options.A: AI tools only work for experts
check_options.B: Anyone can build the same thing quickly with the same tools
check_options.C: Customers no longer want new things
check_options.D: Ideas are now illegal to sell

lesson.check_explanation: Because the tools are shared, building is cheap, so the advantage moves to other things.
